content: Navigational images are not a built-in feature of the MediaWiki software. However, it is possible to configure an image to link to a specific page if desired. Some users find navigating through the instructions on this topic confusing. Here is a more concise explanation: 1. Using Image Redirects: You can apply a redirect on an image page. For instance, on Meta, an internal image link to a page like `Help:Redirect.png` from Commons can be redirected to the Main Page. However, this redirect is not displayed. If the redirect occurs within the same project, a redirect message with a link to the image page (e.g., `MediaWiki:Redirectedfrom`) is inserted on the target page. If you want to use the same image on another page without a redirect or with a different target, you must upload a copy of the image under a different name. 2. Using External Link Format: In projects that allow embedding of external images (which includes most MediaWiki websites except Wikipedia and Meta), you can use the clickpic template. This allows you to link a smaller version of an image to a larger one. For example, if both the small and large images are external, the alternate text displayed will be the name of the image, derived from the last part of the URL. If you control the image, it is recommended to give it a meaningful name, potentially including text like click to enlarge in the name itself. 3. Superimposing Linked Text onto an Image: It is possible to overlay linked text onto an image. For example, you can use a dummy text character (such as a non-breaking space ` `) in a very large font to cover the entire image. This method can be implemented using templates like `Template:Navimg` or `Template:Tim`. However, if the browser is configured to ignore font sizes specified in web pages, only part of the image will link to the specified page, while the rest of the image will link to the image page itself. To verify the target of the link, you can check the hover box or status line when moving the mouse cursor over the image. None of the methods described above work on Wikipedia as of December 2006. For more detailed explanations, refer to the specific sections below.
